Best High-Yield Savings Accounts With No Minimum

If you want to earn more interest on emergency funds or small balances without worrying about a required minimum, you're in the right place. This guide walks through the best high-yield savings account no minimum options, prioritizing easy transfers, low friction account opening, and features that matter for savers with modest balances.

Why “no minimum” and “easy transfers” matter

Many traditional banks require a minimum opening deposit or a minimum daily balance to earn the advertised APY. That excludes people saving small amounts or those who want to start building an emergency fund with whatever they have on hand. A high-yield savings account with no minimum opens the door to higher interest—without a barrier.

Easy transfers are equally important. Seamless transfers between checking and savings (ideally instant or near-instant) let you move cash quickly for bills, emergencies, or investing. For small-balance savers, clunky transfer processes or long ACH holds make a big difference in usefulness.

What to look for in the best high-yield savings account no minimum

  • No minimum balance and no minimum opening deposit: You should be able to open the account and earn APY with any amount.
  • Competitive APY: Look for rates meaningfully above national averages—especially if you plan to leave money long term.
  • Instant or fast transfers: "High yield savings account no minimum instant transfer" is a useful search phrase—look for accounts offering instant transfers to linked checking or debit card push transfers.
  • Low or no fees: Monthly maintenance, inactivity, and outgoing transfer fees can erode returns, particularly on small balances.
  • FDIC or NCUA insurance: Federal insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor-per-institution.
  • Mobile app and online banking quality: For small, frequent moves, easy mobile transfers and automatic savings features are big pluses.
  • External funding/ACH limits: Check if there are limits, holds, or verification steps that slow down transfers.

Top choices for high-yield savings accounts with no minimum

The market changes often, but these account types and providers consistently meet the "no minimum" + "easy transfers" criteria. Always confirm current APYs and terms directly with the bank before opening.

1. Online banks with consistently high APYs

Online-only banks often lead in APY because they have lower overhead. Many offer no minimum balance and easy transfers via ACH or internal instant transfer networks.

  • Digital bank A (example): No minimum opening deposit, competitive APY, instant transfers to a linked checking account if both accounts are with the same bank, and same-day ACH to external banks. Excellent mobile app, no monthly fees.
  • Digital bank B (example): No minimum, slightly lower APY than A but offers debit-card push transfers and same-day transfers when you link to an eligible external bank. Good for frequent micro-savings.

Note: Replace "Digital bank A/B" with the specific provider names when you compare current offers; many large online banks fit this model.

2. Credit unions and neo-banks

Credit unions and fintech “neo-banks” sometimes provide strong APYs with low friction for small savers. Credit unions might require membership eligibility but typically allow low opening balances.

  • Credit union example: No minimum savings account and competitive APY. Membership may be based on geographic area, employer, or association. ACH transfers typically work smoothly after account verification.
  • Neo-bank example: Designed for mobile-first saving, often with instant transfers between products (round-ups, vaults) and easy external transfers via ACH or debit push.

3. Big banks with competitive online savings products

Some major banks have online-only savings products that require no minimums and offer reasonable APYs. They may not always be the top rate leaders, but they provide familiarity and easier transfer options if you already bank with them.

4. Specialized savings platforms

There are platforms that aggregate high-yield savings marketplace accounts or sweep funds into partner banks. These can offer strong rates without minimums and often support instant transfers to an internal checking product.

How to open a high-yield savings account with no minimum — step-by-step

Opening an account should be quick. Follow this checklist to make sure you can start saving immediately and take advantage of instant or rapid transfers:

  1. Choose the account: Compare APY, fees, and transfer options. Confirm "no minimum opening deposit" and read the fine print about receiving the full APY (some accounts require an ACH direct deposit or periodic activity).
  2. Gather your documents: Social Security number or Tax ID, government ID (driver’s license or passport), email, phone number, and physical address.
  3. Open online or in-app: Create an account, verify identity, and read disclosures. Many banks allow instant opening without mailing forms.
  4. Link an external checking account (if desired): For easy transfers, link your primary checking via ACH. Expect a small verification process—micro-deposits or instant verification services (login-based) are common.
  5. Make an initial deposit: Because there’s no minimum, even $1 will work at many banks. Some accounts may require a funding source to start earning APY immediately—confirm the timing.
  6. Confirm transfer methods and limits: Check whether instant transfer is available (debit push, internal transfer), the number of free outgoing transfers, and any daily or monthly ACH limits.

Practical tips for small-balance savers

  • Automate small transfers: Set up automatic weekly transfers of $5–$25. Automation reduces friction and grows your emergency fund without thinking about it.
  • Use round-up features: If available, enable round-up transfers that move spare change into savings. Useful when you can’t commit large amounts.
  • Keep an eye on fees: Even low monthly fees destroy returns on small balances. Prioritize accounts with no maintenance fees and no transfer fees.
  • Leverage instant transfer features: If the account supports instant debit push transfers to your checking debit card, you can access funds faster than standard ACH—helpful for emergencies.
  • Split emergency vs. long-term savings: Use a no-minimum high-yield account for your emergency fund and a different savings or investment vehicle for longer-term goals to optimize liquidity and yield.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Assuming all “high-yield” accounts are the same: APY, fees, transfer options, and customer service vary. Read product terms carefully.
  • Overlooking transfer lag: “No minimum savings account for emergency fund” is only useful if you can access funds quickly. Verify how long transfers take and whether instant options exist.
  • Ignoring insurance: Make sure accounts are FDIC or NCUA insured. Some fintech apps hold funds at partner banks—confirm coverage.
  • Falling for teaser rates: Some banks offer promotional APYs that decline after a period. Check the duration and ongoing rate.
  • Not linking accounts securely: Use verified linking methods (micro-deposits or instant verification) and enable two-factor authentication on your accounts.

Example comparison — what to check when comparing accounts

Use this checklist when you’re comparing options so you don’t miss important differences that matter for small balances and quick access:

  • APY (and whether it’s promotional)
  • Minimum opening deposit (should be $0)
  • Minimum balance requirement to earn APY (should be $0)
  • Fees (monthly, outgoing transfers, ATM, etc.)
  • Transfer options (ACH, instant debit push, internal transfers)
  • Transfer limits and holds (daily/monthly limits, hold times on external transfers)
  • FDIC/NCUA insurance status
  • Mobile app reviews and customer service hours
  • Automatic savings features (round-ups, scheduled transfers, goals)

Who should choose a no-minimum high-yield savings account?

These accounts are ideal for:

  • People starting an emergency fund with small amounts
  • Young savers or those new to banking who don’t have large opening deposits
  • Anyone who wants to park cash temporarily without tying it up or paying fees
  • Savers who need easy transfers between checking and savings—especially instant transfers for liquidity

Final summary and next steps

Finding the best high-yield savings account no minimum comes down to balancing APY, transfer speed, and fees. Online banks, neo-banks, and certain credit unions are often the best places to start. Prioritize accounts that allow instant or fast transfers, have no minimum opening deposit, and charge no monthly fees to protect gains on small balances.

Next steps:

  1. Identify 2–3 providers that meet the no-minimum + easy transfer criteria.
  2. Compare their current APYs, fee schedules, and transfer details side-by-side using the checklist above.
  3. Open the account with your preferred provider, link your checking account, and start an automated savings plan—even $5 per week adds up.

With the right no-minimum high-yield savings account and simple automation, even modest balances can grow faster while remaining easily accessible when you need them.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best high-yield savings account with no minimum?

Look for an online bank offering a competitive APY, no minimum balance, no monthly fee, and FDIC insurance — those terms matter more than chasing the single highest rate.

Are high-yield savings accounts safe?

Yes, at an FDIC-insured bank your money is protected up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank — the same protection as any insured savings account.

Why do online banks offer higher savings rates?

They have no branch network to fund, so they pass the lower overhead to customers as higher APYs and fewer fees.

Can the APY on a HYSA change?

Yes. High-yield savings rates are variable and typically move with the Federal Reserve, so the rate can rise or fall after you open the account.

Is there a limit on savings withdrawals?

Banks may limit certain withdrawal types per month. Check the account terms, though many have relaxed the old six-per-month federal limit.

Best Invoicing Apps for Freelancers With Expense Tracking

Freelancers need two things from their finance tools: fast, professional invoices to get paid and reliable expense tracking to simplify taxes and profit analysis. Use this guide to compare invoice attachments, expense records and receipt scanning. Test the features you need before choosing a free or paid plan.

Which App Lets You Attach Expense Receipts to a Client Invoice?

Zoho Invoice documents both expense receipts and file attachments on invoices. These are separate actions: saving a receipt for your records does not prove the customer can see it.

  1. Record the expense, upload the receipt and associate it with the relevant customer.
  2. Mark the expense as billable if the customer agreed to reimburse it.
  3. Create that customer's invoice and add the billable expense.
  4. Use the invoice's Upload File option if you need to attach the receipt file to the invoice.
  5. Preview the recipient-facing email, portal and PDF with a test invoice before using this workflow with a client. Check exactly which files are visible.

Use the official expense recording guide and invoice attachment instructions. Interfaces and features can vary by edition. This is a documentation-based workflow, not a claim that we tested a paid account.

What freelancers really need from invoicing + expense tracking

  • Simple invoice creation and delivery (PDF + email)
  • Automated reminders and basic payment acceptance (card, ACH, PayPal)
  • Expense capture: receipt photo upload or email receipts, and categorization
  • Basic reporting for profit/loss and tax-ready expense lists
  • Low or no monthly cost, ideally free or a budget that matches your required features
  • Mobile app or easy receipt upload for on-the-go contractors

Big accounting suites often charge more for receipt scanning and separate add-ons. Below are practical, low-cost alternatives that combine invoicing and expense tracking in ways that work for independent contractors, self-employed creators, and consultants.

Top picks: Best invoicing apps for freelancers by workflow and current plan

1) Wave — Check the Receipt-Scanning Subscription

Do not assume receipt scanning is included with free invoicing. Wave lists a separate Receipts subscription and includes scanning in its Pro plan. Invoice attachments and receipt scanning are different features, so check the plan that covers the workflow you need.

Source: Wave receipt and Pro subscription details. Confirm current regional pricing before subscribing.

2) Invoice Ninja — Free plan + affordable paid tier

Why it stands out: Invoice Ninja combines invoicing, proposals, time tracking, and expense management in a compact app. The hosted free tier supports many freelancers; the first paid plan is affordable for teams or heavier use.

  • Expense tracking: Add expenses and attach receipt images; track vendor info and tags.
  • Invoicing: Branded invoices, recurring billing, auto-reminders on paid plans.
  • Pricing: There's a robust free plan; paid hosted plans start in the low range per month.
  • Best for: Freelancers who want optional upgrades (client portals, more automations) but prefer a strong free base.
  • Drawback: UX can feel more technical compared with consumer-oriented apps.

3) Zoho Invoice — Powerful free invoicing with expense features

Why it stands out: Zoho Invoice is part of the Zoho suite and offers a generous free invoicing product with expense logging and receipt attachment. It’s intuitive and integrates with other Zoho products if you scale later.

  • Expense tracking: Record expenses, attach receipts, and convert billable expenses into invoices.
  • Invoicing: Custom templates, recurring invoices, and client portal options.
  • Best for: Self-employed users who want a polished UI and optional integrations without a big cost.
  • Drawback: Payment processing and advanced business features may involve transaction fees or upgrades.

4) ZipBooks — Simple free invoicing + light expense tracking

Why it stands out: ZipBooks provides clean invoice templates, easy bookkeeping basics, and expense entry on its free tier. It's a good lightweight alternative if you want a tidy dashboard and painless setup.

  • Expense tracking: Manually add expenses and upload receipts; categorize for reports.
  • Invoicing: Unlimited invoices on free plan; simple reporting and customer management.
  • Best for: Freelancers who prioritize an easy UI and quick onboarding.
  • Drawback: Some reporting and bank reconciliation features require paid tiers.

5) PayPal Invoicing — Free invoicing; pay-per-transaction

Why it stands out: If you already rely on PayPal for payments, PayPal Invoicing lets you send invoices for free and capture payments quickly. Expense tracking is more manual—use PayPal transaction history or link with a separate receipt app—but combined solutions keep costs near zero.

  • Expense tracking: Not native—use exported transaction lists or pair with a free expense app.
  • Invoicing: Create, send, and track invoices for free; client pays with PayPal or card (fees apply).
  • Best for: Contractors who prioritize payment speed and are okay handling receipts separately.
  • Drawback: Limited native expense management; best combined with another free receipt capture tool.

How to choose the right app for your freelance business

Use this short checklist to match a tool to your workflow and budget.

  • Do you need full bookkeeping or just expense lists for taxes? If just expenses, a simple free invoice app with receipt upload (Zoho Invoice) may be enough; check the workflow in your edition.
  • Do you want mobile receipt capture? Make sure the app’s mobile experience is smooth—Wave and Invoice Ninja offer mobile-friendly upload.
  • Do you want payment processing inside the same app? If yes, check transaction fees and supported payment methods.
  • How many clients or invoices per month? Some free plans cap features; if you bill dozens of clients, confirm limits.
  • Do you need integrations (PayPal, Stripe, bank import)? Integrations can save manual data entry and reduce errors.

Step-by-step: Setting up a cheap invoicing + expense workflow

Here is a workflow to test with your chosen app before sending a client invoice. <$10/month app.

  1. Choose an app: Pick one from the list above based on mobile capture, payment needs, and UI preference.
  2. Create your account and add business details: logo, address, tax ID (if needed), and default payment terms.
  3. Connect payment processing: Link Stripe, PayPal, or bank transfer options so clients can pay directly from invoices.
  4. Set up expense categories: Create categories like Travel, Supplies, Subcontractors, Meals, and Software for tax time.
  5. Install mobile app and test receipt capture: Snap a receipt, attach it to an expense, and mark whether it’s billable to a client.
  6. Create an invoice template: Save a template with your branding, payment terms, and itemized rates for common services.
  7. Automate reminders and late fees: Turn on reminders to reduce follow-ups; add a modest late fee if desired.
  8. Run month-end reports: Export expenses and invoice income to prepare quarterly taxes or hand off to an accountant.

Practical tips and examples

  • Example workflow: For each client project, create a project folder in the app. Mark expenses as billable when they relate to that project. At month-end, convert billable expenses to an invoice to ensure you’re reimbursed.
  • Receipts: Photograph receipts immediately. Most apps attach images to expenses; keep descriptive notes (e.g., “Client lunch with X — project Y”).
  • Tax time: Use expense categories consistently. That saves hours when you or your accountant prepares Schedule C or other tax forms.
  • Mix-and-match: If an app lacks a feature, use a small dedicated expense scanner (free iOS/Android apps) and import CSVs into your invoicing tool monthly.
  • Backups: Export invoices and expenses quarterly as CSV or PDF for redundancy.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Thinking a “free” app means no fees: Even free invoicing tools usually charge payment processing fees when clients pay by card. Factor that into your rates.
  • Skipping receipt photos: Trying to reconstruct expenses later wastes time and can increase audit risk. Snap receipts promptly.
  • Not categorizing expenses: Unsorted expenses make tax prep painful. Create and use consistent categories from day one.
  • Keeping everything in separate apps: Using one tool for invoicing and expense tracking reduces reconciliation work and errors.
  • Choosing features you don’t use: Don’t pay for advanced workflows (project management, payroll) you’ll never use. Stick to invoicing + expense tracking if that’s all you need.

Quick comparison summary

  • Wave — Check the current invoicing and receipt-scanning plans separately.
  • Invoice Ninja — Great free tier with optional low-cost upgrades; strong if you want time tracking and proposals bundled.
  • Zoho Invoice — Polished UI, strong expense capture and easy conversions of expenses into invoices.
  • ZipBooks — Simple, clean, and easy for freelancers who want minimal setup.
  • PayPal Invoicing — Fast payments if you prioritize quick client payments; pair with a free receipt app for expenses.

Final checklist before you commit

  • Mobile receipt capture works reliably.
  • Payment methods you prefer are supported and fees acceptable.
  • Export options exist for taxes/accounting (CSV or PDF).
  • Recurring invoices and reminders are available if you bill retainer clients.
  • Upgrading later is affordable and adds only the features you’ll use.

Conclusion

Finding the best invoicing app for freelancers with expense tracking free (or a budget that matches your required features) is achievable. Wave, Invoice Ninja, Zoho Invoice, and ZipBooks each offer low-cost routes to professional invoicing plus receipt and expense management. Choose the one that matches your workflow—prioritizing mobile receipt capture, integrated payments, and reliable reporting—and set it up with consistent categories and a quick monthly export routine. That way you’ll spend less time hunting receipts and more time doing billable work.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best invoicing app with expense tracking for freelancers?

An app that captures receipts, categorizes expenses, and exports a tax summary alongside professional invoicing — so your income and deductions live in one place.

Why track expenses inside your invoicing app?

Keeping invoices and expenses together means every deductible cost is logged as you go, so Schedule C and quarterly taxes are quick instead of a year-end scramble.

Can invoicing apps track mileage?

Some do, either automatically via your phone's GPS or by manual entry — useful for claiming the IRS standard mileage deduction if you drive for work.

Do freelancers really need expense tracking?

If you claim business deductions, yes — the IRS expects records. Keep records and confirm tax treatment with a qualified professional; automation does not establish deductibility.

Is free expense-tracking software good enough?

Free tiers handle basic receipt logging and invoicing for low-volume freelancers. Paid plans add automation, reports, and accounting sync as your work grows.

Opening is usually straightforward if you have the right documents. Follow this checklist to finish the process in one session with minimal delays.

  1. Confirm your LLC’s paperwork — Articles of Organization (or Certificate of Formation) and Employer Identification Number (EIN). Some banks allow single-member LLCs to use the owner’s SSN, but an EIN is recommended.
  2. Prepare owner ID and contact details — government-issued ID (driver’s license or passport), email, phone number, and home/business address.
  3. Operating Agreement and Ownership Information — many banks request your LLC operating agreement and a list of members/owners with ownership percentages.
  4. Decide account signers — who will have online access and who will be authorized signers on checks.
  5. Start the online application — choose the bank that matches your needs, select the business checking product, and complete the digital form while uploading documents.
  6. Fund the account — most banks require an initial deposit (often low or $0 for no-fee accounts). Transfer from a personal account, wire, or mobile deposit where supported.
  7. Set up digital tools — enable online banking, connect accounting software, set up ACH for payroll or inbound payments, order debit cards, and configure alerts.

Practical tips and examples

  • If you’re a single-member LLC: Novo and BlueVine are very friendly for sole proprietors and single-member LLCs and typically do not require in-person visits.
  • If you need developer tools or multiple subaccounts: Mercury’s subaccount and API capabilities help startups split funds (e.g., payroll vs. operating expenses) without multiple bank relationships.
  • Want free transfers: Confirm that the account includes free ACH transfers and outgoing domestic ACH; some banks charge for outgoing wires but not ACH.
  • ATM access: Online-only banks may use ATM networks and reimburse fees up to a limit — verify the reimbursement policy if cash access matters.
  • Integration considerations: If you use Stripe, Square, QuickBooks, or a payroll provider, check native integrations to save manual uploads.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Misconception: “No monthly fee means zero fees.” Many no-monthly-fee accounts still charge for wire transfers, international transactions, or cash deposits. Read the fine print for per-item fees.
  • Mistake: Using a personal bank for business. Mixing personal and business funds can hurt liability protection and complicate bookkeeping and taxes. Open a dedicated LLC business checking account as soon as possible.
  • Mistake: Choosing solely for APY. High APY is nice but not at the expense of banking functionality. Prioritize free transfers, integrations, and easy onboarding.
  • Mistake: Not verifying online onboarding rules for your specific LLC type. Foreign-owned LLCs, multi-member LLCs, or series LLCs sometimes face additional documentation or are ineligible for some online-only banks.
  • Mistake: Overlooking transfer limits and hold times. Some banks place holds on large deposits or limit same-day outbound transfers for new accounts. Check policies if you expect high volumes early on.

Checklist: What to confirm before you apply

  • Does the account truly have no monthly maintenance fee?
  • Are incoming and outgoing ACH transfers free?
  • Is online account opening available for your LLC type?
  • What documentation will the bank require to verify your business?
  • Are there transaction limits, ATM fees, or wire fees that could affect you?
  • Does the bank integrate with your accounting and payment tools?

Final recommendation: How to pick the best fit

If your priority is the best business checking account for new LLC with no monthly fee and an easy online setup, start by shortlisting 2–3 banks from the suggestions above and compare them using the checklist. If you want a simple, no-friction solution with solid integrations, Novo or BlueVine are excellent first choices. If your LLC is a startup or you expect multiple users and programmatic transfers, Mercury is an outstanding option. For a more traditional banking relationship with no fees and unlimited transactions, nbkc and Axos are strong contenders.

Conclusion

Opening a no monthly fee business checking account for a new LLC can be straightforward when you know what to look for: true fee-free maintenance, free ACH transfers, clear online onboarding, and compatibility with your business tools. Use the step-by-step checklist above, compare the short list of recommended providers, and avoid common mistakes (like mixing personal and business funds). With the right account, you’ll keep costs low, maintain clean records, and focus on growing your LLC.

What is the best business checking account for a new LLC?

One with no monthly fee, no minimum balance, free ACH, and a debit card — so a pre-revenue LLC keeps costs at zero while separating business funds.

What documents does a new LLC need to open a bank account?

Typically your EIN, articles of organization, an operating agreement (for multi-member LLCs), and photo ID for the owners.

Does an LLC need an EIN to open a bank account?

Yes. Unlike sole proprietors, LLCs generally must provide an EIN — it's free from the IRS and takes minutes to obtain online.

You shouldn't. Mixing personal and LLC funds can undermine the liability protection an LLC provides and complicates taxes and bookkeeping.

Multi-member LLCs are more likely to be asked for an operating agreement; both need an EIN and formation documents.

You can create unlimited invoices, send them by email, and accept payments via credit card or bank transfer (ACH). Wave also offers integrated accounting and receipt scanning, which adds value without recurring costs.

  • Price: Free for invoicing and accounting; payment processing fees apply
  • Key features: Unlimited invoices, customizable templates, basic reporting, integrated accounting
  • Drawbacks: No advanced automation or client portal on the free plan; payment fees charged per transaction

2. Zoho Invoice — Full-featured free tier with automation

Why it’s good: Zoho Invoice has a robust free tier for small freelancers, offering client portals, recurring invoices, time tracking, and automated payment reminders. The interface is clean and integrates well with other Zoho apps if you grow into a broader ecosystem later.

  • Price: Free for many users on the standalone Zoho Invoice plan (check current limits)
  • Key features: Client portal, recurring billing, expense tracking, multi-currency support
  • Drawbacks: Some advanced features are gated behind paid Zoho plans; UI may be feature-rich for very simple users

3. Invoice Ninja — Low-cost plan for growing freelancers

Why it’s good: Invoice Ninja offers a generous free plan and a paid Pro plan that often sits around $10/month. It supports proposals, invoices, client portals, time tracking, and multiple integrations. For freelancers who want a professional client portal and automation but can’t exceed $10/month, Invoice Ninja is a strong contender.

  • Price: Free tier available; Pro plans often start at roughly $10/month (confirm current pricing)
  • Key features: Client portal, recurring invoices, payment gateways, proposals, time tracking
  • Drawbacks: The free plan has limits on features and branding; self-hosting option exists but requires technical setup

4. Square Invoices — Simple, no-monthly-fee invoicing with POS tie-in

Why it’s good: Square Invoices is free to use—no monthly fee—making it ideal for freelancers who need straightforward invoice sending and fast payment via Square. It’s particularly useful if you already use Square for in-person payments.

  • Price: No monthly fee; transaction fees apply when clients pay with card
  • Key features: Simple invoice builder, recurring invoices, estimates, built-in payment processing
  • Drawbacks: Limited advanced accounting features; transaction fees can add up

5. PayPal Invoicing — Cheap invoicing with familiar payments

Why it’s good: If many clients already use PayPal, its invoicing is a lightweight choice—no monthly subscription and easy online payment for clients. PayPal is ideal for freelancers who need simple invoices and fast acceptance by clients internationally.

  • Price: No monthly fee; PayPal transaction fees per payment
  • Key features: Create and send invoices, recurring payments, mobile-friendly
  • Drawbacks: Higher transaction fees for international or credit card payments; limited reporting

How to choose between free and paid (< $10/month) plans

When comparing these affordable invoicing apps for freelancers, follow this decision process:

  1. List must-have features: client portal, recurring invoices, tax/expense tracking, or online payments.
  2. Estimate monthly transaction volume: If you bill a lot and are charged per-transaction, a low monthly fee might reduce overall costs.
  3. Check client expectations: Some clients prefer a portal to view past invoices or make payments—if that matters, prioritize tools with a client portal.
  4. Confirm payment gateway compatibility: Ensure Stripe, PayPal, or Square integrations match your and your clients’ preferences.
  5. Test the free tier first: Many apps let you try features before upgrading. Start free and only pay if you miss automation or limits.

This way you’ll avoid paying for features you don’t need while keeping your process efficient.

Practical setup: How to get started in under 30 minutes

Here’s a simple step-by-step setup you can complete quickly with most inexpensive invoicing tools:

  1. Create an account and verify your email.
  2. Add your business name, logo, contact information, and payment details (Stripe/PayPal/Square).
  3. Set up tax rates and default invoice terms (e.g., Net 15 or Net 30) and a late fee policy if you use one.
  4. Create a client profile with billing address and preferred payment method.
  5. Build an invoice template—add logo, itemized services, rates, and payment instructions.
  6. Send a test invoice to yourself to check the PDF, email content, and payment flow.
  7. Enable automated reminders and recurring invoices if you have retainer clients.

Once set up, use an invoice numbering system and save exported reports periodically for taxes.

Tips for speeding up payments and using cheap invoicing software effectively

  • Offer multiple online payment options to remove friction—card, bank transfer, or PayPal.
  • Set clear payment terms and mention due dates on every invoice.
  • Include a concise description of work and attach deliverables or time logs if relevant.
  • Automate reminders—late fees sometimes motivate quicker payments, but use them sparingly to preserve client relationships.
  • Send invoices promptly: invoices sent within a day of delivery get paid faster than those delayed.
  • Keep a simple “Payment Instructions” section on each invoice listing preferred methods and any processing fees.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

Mistake: Choosing the cheapest tool without checking payment fees

Many freelancers assume “free” equals low cost. But payment processing fees (often 2.9% + a fixed fee) can make a free platform more expensive per transaction. Calculate projected monthly transaction fees to compare real costs.

Mistake: Overlooking client experience

If your client finds the invoice confusing or the payment process clunky, you risk slower payments. Prioritize clarity and a clean client portal over unnecessary bells and whistles.

Mistake: Skipping data export/backups

Relying only on the cloud without regular exports can cause trouble during audits or if you switch platforms. Export invoices and client lists periodically (CSV/PDF).

Misconception: Paid plans always mean better support

Support quality varies. Some free tools offer solid community help and clear self-service documentation. Check support channels (email, chat, phone) and response expectations before you commit.

Quick comparison checklist: Which solution fits you?

  • If you want truly free invoicing with basic accounting: choose Wave.
  • If you need a client portal, recurring invoices, and automation without monthly cost: try Zoho Invoice.
  • If you want a low-cost upgrade option that adds portals and proposals: Invoice Ninja is a top pick.
  • If you want minimal setup and fast payments with POS integration: Square Invoices fits well.
  • If many clients already use PayPal or prefer PayPal payments: use PayPal Invoicing for convenience.

Example invoice workflow for a freelancer

Here’s an example use-case for a freelance designer billing $1,200 monthly retainer and occasional project work:

  1. Use Zoho Invoice (free) to create a client profile and enable the client portal.
  2. Create a recurring invoice for the $1,200 retainer, set to auto-send on the 1st of each month.
  3. For a one-off project, generate a separate invoice with time-logged line items and attach final deliverables as a ZIP or Google Drive link.
  4. Enable Stripe and PayPal so the client can choose their payment method; allow ACH for lower fees if available.
  5. If a payment is late, automated reminder emails send after 7 and 14 days; follow up with a friendly personal email if needed.
  6. Export monthly income reports and save them to your accounting folder for tax season.

Final thoughts and quick summary

Finding the best invoicing software for freelancers under $10/month is very possible—many capable options are free or cost just a few dollars. Wave and Zoho Invoice are excellent starting points for sole proprietors and freelancers who want strong free features. Invoice Ninja is a great choice if you need a low-cost upgrade that adds client portals and automation. Square and PayPal offer convenient, no-subscription invoicing if you prioritize payment simplicity.

Choose based on the features you actually use (client portal, recurring invoices, integrations), calculate total transaction costs, and start with a free trial when available. With the right affordable invoicing tool, you can spend less time on billing and more time on your craft—without exceeding a tight monthly budget.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best free invoicing software for freelancers?

Several tools offer free, unlimited professional invoicing and let clients pay by card through Stripe or PayPal — enough for most low-volume freelancers.

Do freelancers really need invoicing software?

It isn't mandatory, but it gets you paid faster with automatic reminders and keeps clean records for tax time — a big time-saver over manual invoices.

Can invoicing software accept card payments?

Yes. Most tools integrate Stripe or PayPal so clients can pay a card or bank transfer directly from the invoice; a small processing fee applies.

What should a freelance invoice include?

Your name/business details, the client's details, an invoice number and date, itemised work, the total, payment terms, and your tax ID where required.

Is invoicing software worth paying for?

If you send more than a handful of invoices a month, paid tiers pay for themselves through automation, reminders, and expense/tax tracking.

  • Best Checking Account for Freelancers with Irregular Income
  • Top invoicing app for freelancers with expense tracking free

Also check the monthly fee and any waiver conditions, transaction limits, whether the account is opened in the business name, and whether the account fits how your LLC will actually receive and send money. Always confirm the current terms with the bank before opening an account.

Questions to ask before opening

Before you open an account, ask the bank these questions and check the answers in the current terms and fee schedule. Is incoming ACH free, and is outgoing ACH free as well, or priced separately? What is the monthly fee, and is it waived only if you meet a balance or transaction condition? Are there limits on the number or value of ACH transfers, deposits, or other transactions each month? Best Business Checking for New LLCs — No Fee & Free ACH

Starting an LLC is exciting, but choosing the right bank account is a foundational step that affects cash flow, taxes, and professionalism. If you're searching for the best business checking account for new LLC no monthly fee free ACH, this guide compares the top options, explains what to look for, and offers practical tips so your single-member or multi-member LLC gets a low-cost, easy-to-manage account with free ACH transfers.

Why no monthly fee and free ACH matter for new LLCs

New businesses often have tight budgets and unpredictable income. Two account features matter more than most:

  • No monthly fee: Eliminates a recurring drain on cash flow and reduces the need to meet balance or transaction thresholds to avoid charges.
  • Free ACH transfers: Enables low-cost payments and payroll, vendor payments, and customer refunds. ACH is far cheaper than wire transfers or paper checks for recurring or batch payments.

Combining both means your LLC avoids routine banking costs while keeping payment options flexible—ideal for startups or single-member LLCs that want to minimize overhead.

What to look for besides no fee and free ACH

While the primary search intent centers on no-fee accounts with free ACH, a few additional features are important to compare:

  • Monthly transaction limits: Some "free" accounts limit the number of free transactions or deposits.
  • Mobile and online banking quality: Good mobile apps, ACH initiation, and integrations with accounting software (QuickBooks, Xero) save time.
  • Inbound vs outbound ACH policies: Ensure both types are free or that outbound ACH (payments you send) isn’t charged.
  • Cash deposit capability: Physical businesses may need branches or cash deposit options.
  • Integration and API for scaling: If you plan to automate payments or use payroll services, check for APIs or developer tools.
  • Customer support and fraud controls: Look for same-day support and positive fraud protection features.

Account Types to Compare for a New LLC

These are account categories and examples to investigate, not verified free-account offers. Confirm current fees, eligibility and transfer terms with each provider.

1. Online challenger banks and fintech accounts (e.g., Novo, BlueVine, Mercury)

  • Why they stand out: Many fintech business accounts offer no monthly fee and include free ACH transfers. They typically provide excellent integrations for startups and single-member LLCs.
  • Strengths: Check the interface, onboarding requirements, ACH debit and credit fees, accounting integrations and fees for the services your LLC needs.
  • Limitations: Cash deposits are often difficult or expensive. Ask which bank holds the funds and where the deposit-insurance conditions are documented.
  • Best for: Remote-first single-member LLCs, SaaS startups, freelancers who accept ACH and don’t need cash handling.

2. Traditional regional banks offering no-fee business checking

  • Why they stand out: Some regional banks and credit unions provide no-fee business checking with free ACH, often with better access to in-person services and cash deposit options.
  • Strengths: Local relationship banking, branch and ATM access, often free ACH for smaller businesses, more personalized service.
  • Limitations: Monthly limits on free transactions or minimum balance requirements might apply. Online tools can be less polished than fintechs.
  • Best for: New LLCs that anticipate cash transactions, want local lending relationships, or prefer in-person service.

3. Big national banks with small-business products (promos and conditions vary)

  • Why they stand out: Large banks sometimes waive monthly fees if you maintain a low minimum balance or sign up for qualifying services; ACH is often included but watch the fine print.
  • Strengths: Widespread branch networks, broad product suites (loans, merchant services), and robust fraud protection.
  • Limitations: Monthly fee waivers commonly require balances or linked accounts; some charge for ACH or impose limits. New LLCs may face stricter documentation rules.
  • Best for: Businesses that plan to scale, need a full-service bank, or want immediate access to business lending later on.

Before Applying: Documents and ACH Questions

The SBA business-bank-account guide lists common documents such as tax identification, formation documents, ownership agreements and business licenses. Ask the chosen bank which documents apply to your LLC and its signers.

Use this checklist when comparing accounts with no monthly fee and free ACH:

  • Is the monthly fee unconditionally zero, or is there a waiver requirement?
  • Are incoming ACH credits, outgoing payments and collection debits priced separately?
  • What are the standard and same-day transfer charges, limits and cut-off times?
  • Are payroll, cash deposits, returned payments or accounting integrations separate services?
  • Does the account support your owners' locations, business activity and expected transaction volume?

Save the provider's current fee schedule and note the date checked. A free transfer allowance is not a promise that every payment service is free.

Quick comparison checklist

Use this checklist when evaluating accounts to find the best bank account for single-member LLC startups or multi-member LLCs:

  • Is there a monthly fee? If yes, what are waiver conditions?
  • Are inbound and outbound ACH transfers free? Are there per-month limits?
  • Are there fees for same-day ACH or payroll ACH?
  • Does the bank provide integration with your accounting software or payment platforms?
  • Are there limits on cash deposits or fees for them?
  • How easy is account opening for a newly formed LLC? (Some banks require an EIN, Articles of Organization, or operating agreement.)
  • What is the customer support and fraud protection level?

Practical examples: Which account fits which LLC?

Here are some real-world scenarios to help you decide:

  • Solo consultant operating remotely: Compare remote-friendly accounts using their current fee schedules, ACH limits and invoicing integrations; do not infer these terms from the provider name.
  • Retail pop-up or local service business that handles cash: A regional bank or credit union with free business checking and branch access is better for depositing cash and building local lending relationships.
  • New LLC planning to hire employees quickly: Choose an account that offers free outbound ACH for payroll or integrates with payroll processors. Confirm whether same-day ACH costs extra.
  • High transaction volume startup: Look for unlimited free ACH and low per-transaction fees; some fintechs or business banks have plans tailored to higher volume.

How to open a no-fee business checking for new LLCs

Opening an account is straightforward, but new LLCs should prepare these documents to avoid delays:

  • Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS; single-member LLCs sometimes can open with a Social Security Number but EIN is recommended.
  • Articles of Organization (LLC formation documents) filed with your state.
  • Operating Agreement (especially for multi-member LLCs) to show authorized signers.
  • Valid government-issued ID for all owners/authorized signers.
  • Initial deposit (if required). Confirm the provider’s opening-deposit requirement and review process.

Tip: Ask the bank upfront whether newly-formed LLCs can open accounts online or if you must visit a branch. Fintechs often allow fully remote onboarding in minutes.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Assuming “no monthly fee” means no fees at all: Check for transaction fees, cash deposit fees, outgoing wire fees, and charges for same-day ACH or expedited services.
  • Ignoring ACH limits: Some banks cap the number of free ACH transfers per month; exceeding them may incur charges.
  • Overvaluing branch access if you never deposit cash: For online-only businesses, fintech accounts can be cheaper and faster.
  • Not checking integration options: If you use QuickBooks, Stripe, Gusto, or other tools, ensure the bank integrates smoothly to save reconciliation time.
  • Failing to separate personal and business funds: Even single-member LLCs should maintain a dedicated business checking to preserve liability protection and simplify taxes.

Practical tips to maximize a free ACH business bank account for LLC

  • Automate recurring bills with outbound ACH to avoid late fees and reduce check costs.
  • Use accounting integrations to reconcile deposits and ACH payments automatically.
  • Monitor monthly transaction limits and prioritize ACH over card payments where cheaper.
  • Keep minimum balances if required for fee waivers—but don’t overfund an idle account. Consider a sweep to an interest-bearing account if available.
  • Document all signers and ownership to prevent delays when adding personnel or changing accounts.

How to choose between fintech vs. traditional bank for new LLC checking

Ask yourself these questions:

  • Do I need to deposit cash often?
  • Do I value in-person service or branch lending relationships?
  • Will I rely on payroll and same-day ACH frequently?
  • Do I want fast digital onboarding and strong API/integration support?

If you answer “yes” to cash or branch needs, a regional bank or credit union may suit you. If you prioritize low fees, quick setup, and automation, a fintech or challenger bank is often the best business checking for single-member LLC startups.

Conclusion

For new LLCs seeking the best business checking account for new LLC no monthly fee free ACH, fintech business accounts and many regional banks often meet that need. The ideal choice depends on whether your LLC needs cash handling, branch access, or advanced digital integrations. Use the checklist above to compare accounts on fees, ACH policies, cash services, and integrations. Open with clear documentation (EIN, Articles of Organization, IDs), and separate business finances from personal funds to preserve liability protection.

Start by shortlisting a few accounts that explicitly advertise no monthly fee and free ACH transfers, verify any transaction caps or same-day ACH charges, and test the onboarding process. That approach will get your new LLC a cost-effective, professional banking setup that supports growth without unnecessary expenses.

Frequently asked questions

What is a business checking account with free ACH?

An account that lets you send and receive ACH bank transfers at no charge — ideal for paying contractors and getting paid by clients without per-transfer fees.

Is ACH free on business accounts?

At many online banks, yes — both incoming and outgoing ACH are free. Traditional banks sometimes charge per transfer or for higher volumes, so check the terms.

What's the difference between ACH and a wire?

ACH is a low-cost bank-to-bank transfer that settles in 1-3 days; wires are same-day but usually cost $15-30. Use ACH for routine payments, wires for urgent ones.

How long does an ACH transfer take?

Standard ACH typically settles in one to three business days. Some banks offer same-day ACH for an extra fee.

Are there limits on ACH transfers?

Yes, banks set daily and monthly ACH limits that vary by account and history. Check the limits if you make large or frequent payments.

Mortgage Tips for Freelancers: First-Time Homebuyer Guide

Getting a mortgage as a freelancer or gig worker can feel complicated—but it's entirely possible with the right preparation. Lenders look for consistent income, reasonable debt levels, and documentation they can rely on. This guide walks you through practical, step-by-step strategies to qualify for a mortgage for freelancers first-time home buyer applicants, covering what documents lenders need from self-employed borrowers, loan options, and actionable tips to improve approval chances.

Why lenders treat freelancers differently

Lenders underwrite mortgages based on the borrower’s ability to repay. For W-2 employees, that’s usually straightforward: regular pay stubs and employer confirmation. Freelancers and gig workers, however, often have variable income, multiple clients, and nontraditional tax filings. Because of that variability, lenders require more documentation and look for proof that your freelance income is stable and likely to continue.

Understanding what lenders want will help you present a clear income picture and avoid common pitfalls.

Step-by-step path to qualify: from preparation to closing

Step 1 — Stabilize and document your income (12–24 months)

  • Build a consistent income track record. Many lenders prefer 24 months of self-employment history; some consider 12 months if you have prior W-2 income or strong reserves.
  • Keep clean business and personal finances. Use a business account for client payments and avoid mixing personal and business expenses.
  • Reduce large swings in income where possible. If you can smooth receipts (retainer agreements, recurring contracts), that helps underwriters see stability.

Step 2 — Organize required documentation

Being organized speeds up the underwriting process. Below is a checklist of documents lenders need from self-employed borrowers. Different lenders or loan programs may request additional items, but this covers the essentials.

  • Personal tax returns (Form 1040) for the last 2 years—signed and complete
  • Business tax returns (Form 1120, 1120-S, or Schedule C) for the last 2 years
  • Profit and loss statement (P&L) for the current year—preferably year-to-date and prepared by you or an accountant
  • Bank statements—typically 2–12 months for both business and personal accounts
  • 1099s for the last 1–2 years (if applicable)
  • Client contracts, invoices, or signed letters confirming ongoing work or expected income
  • Proof of assets and reserves (savings, investments, retirement accounts)
  • Valid ID and Social Security number
  • Explanation letters for any large deposits, gaps in income, or one-time write-offs

Tip: Lenders often want tax returns with all schedules attached. Don’t strip out Schedule C or other schedules that show business losses or expenses—these tell the full income story.

Step 3 — Choose the right loan program

First-time home buyer loan options for gig economy workers vary by program and lender. Here are common options and how they fit freelancers.

  • Conventional loans (Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac) – Typically require 2 years of consistent income. Debt-to-income (DTI) ratios and credit scores are important. Flexible for self-employed borrowers if documentation is strong.
  • FHA loans – More forgiving on credit scores and down payments (as low as 3.5%), but lenders still want stable income and 2 years of tax returns in most cases.
  • VA loans – Available to eligible veterans and service members and can be used by self-employed applicants; service requirements, credit, and residual income tests apply.
  • USDA loans – For eligible rural areas; can be used by self-employed borrowers with proper documentation.
  • Bank statement mortgage programs – Alternative qualifying method using 12–24 months of bank statements (personal and/or business) instead of tax returns. Good if you have significant deductions that lower taxable income but steady cash flow.
  • Stated income or portfolio loans – Less common and higher cost. Lenders rely more on assets and credit rather than documented income; often used by high-net-worth self-employed borrowers.

Choosing the right program depends on your credit profile, down payment, and how your income appears on tax returns. Shop multiple lenders—some specialize in self-employed mortgages.

Step 4 — Improve credit and reduce debt

  • Check your credit report and correct errors. Get copies from the three bureaus and dispute inaccuracies early.
  • Pay down high-interest debt to lower your DTI. Even reducing credit card balances can improve your qualifying ratio.
  • Aim for a credit score aligned with your chosen program: 620+ for many conventional loans, 580+ for many FHA loans, and higher scores for best rates.
  • Avoid large new debts or co-signing for loans during the mortgage process; new obligations can kill approval.

Step 5 — Build reserves and a solid down payment

Lenders like seeing cash reserves—months of mortgage payments saved—especially for self-employed borrowers. If your tax returns show low net income due to deductions, strong reserves can reassure lenders that you can handle payments.

  • Save at least 2–6 months of mortgage payments as reserves; more is better if you have variable income.
  • Reduce reliance on gifted down payments—lenders may require a season of the funds in your account or documentation explaining the gift source.

Step 6 — Get preapproved by the right lender

Preapproval is not a guarantee, but a thorough preapproval from a lender experienced with freelancers helps you understand what you can afford and demonstrates seriousness to sellers. Ask lenders how they verify self-employed income: tax returns, bank statement programs, or other methods.

Practical tips to improve mortgage approval chances as a freelancer

  • Work with an accountant experienced in mortgage applications. They can prepare clean P&Ls and explain business deductions that might otherwise hurt your qualifying income.
  • Avoid over-reporting deductions if you can legitimately reduce them; high write-offs lower your qualifying income. Talk to your tax advisor about timing business expenses.
  • Use year-to-date profit and loss statements to show recent income increases—some lenders will consider current-year improvement if documented.
  • Consider locking in long-term contracts or retainer agreements with clients and keep copies to show underwriters.
  • Choose lenders that advertise self-employed mortgage requirements 2026 or specifically market to freelancers—those lenders understand modern gig economy income streams.
  • Leverage bank statement loans if your tax returns don’t reflect your cash flow due to legitimate write-offs.
  • If you recently transitioned from W-2 to freelance, keep W-2 history and show continuity of income from the same industry.
  • Document large deposits. Lenders will ask for explanations and proof for any significant incoming funds in your accounts.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Assuming one lender represents all lenders: Policies vary. If one lender declines you, another might approve you with different documentation requirements.
  • Hiding or not explaining deductions: Underwriters expect deductions. Provide clear records and, when needed, explanation letters describing one-time expenses.
  • Ignoring tax returns: Even with bank-statement programs, tax returns often remain part of the file. Never omit required tax documentation.
  • Maxing out credit: Using credit cards heavily before applying raises red flags. Pay down balances and avoid new credit inquiries.
  • Failing to show reserves: Relying solely on projected income without demonstrating reserves can hurt approval odds for freelancers.

Real-world examples

Example 1: Freelancer with high gross income but low taxable income

  • Situation: A graphic designer earns $120k gross but reports $55k taxable income on Schedule C due to equipment purchases and business travel.
  • Strategy: Use a bank-statement mortgage program to prove the $120k cash flow, present contracts, and show 6 months of mortgage reserves to offset low taxable income.

Example 2: New freelancer with 12 months of income

  • Situation: A consultant left a W-2 job 14 months ago and has 12 months of freelance 1099 income.
  • Strategy: Lenders may consider the 12-month history if combined with previous W-2 income in the same field. Provide contracts, current P&L, and a letter showing ongoing client commitments.

How to talk to lenders—questions to ask

  • Which documentation do you require for self-employed applicants? (Ask specifically about tax returns vs. bank statements.)
  • Do you offer bank statement loan programs or alternative income verification options?
  • What minimum months of reserves do you require for self-employed borrowers?
  • How do you handle business losses and pass-through entity income?
  • What credit score and DTI targets do you use for first-time home buyers who are self-employed?

Checklist before submitting a mortgage application

  • Collected 2 years of complete tax returns and 12–24 months of bank statements
  • Prepared an up-to-date profit & loss statement and balance sheet (if applicable)
  • Reduced credit card balances and checked credit reports for errors
  • Saved 2–6 months of mortgage payments as reserves
  • Gathered client contracts, invoices, and letters confirming future work
  • Consulted an accountant about any large deductions or write-offs
  • Spoken with at least two lenders experienced with freelancers

Conclusion

Mortgage for freelancers first-time home buyer applicants is achievable with careful planning, organized documentation, and the right lender. Stabilize your income, keep tidy financial records, prepare tax returns and bank statements, and consider alternative loan programs if your taxable income doesn’t reflect your cash flow. Work with an accountant and lenders who understand gig economy income, and follow the step-by-step checklist above to improve your approval chances.

Start by gathering your last two years of tax returns, a current profit and loss statement, and 12 months of bank statements. Then shop lenders and ask targeted questions about self-employed mortgage requirements 2026 and beyond. With preparation, you can move from freelance uncertainty to first-time homebuyer confidence.

Frequently asked questions

Can a freelancer get a mortgage?

Yes. Self-employed borrowers qualify by documenting income — usually two years of tax returns — plus credit score, down payment, and debt-to-income like any borrower.

How many years of self-employment do you need for a mortgage?

Most conventional lenders want two years of self-employment income history, though some accept one year with a strong prior work record in the same field.

Do tax write-offs hurt mortgage approval?

They can. Lenders qualify you on net income after deductions, so aggressive write-offs lower your documented income and the loan amount you qualify for.

What is a bank-statement mortgage?

A loan that verifies income from 12-24 months of bank deposits instead of tax returns — useful for freelancers with strong cash flow but low taxable income, usually at higher rates.

How can freelancers improve their mortgage approval odds?

Raise your credit score, lower debt-to-income, save a larger down payment, keep two years of clean records, and avoid big new debts before applying.

Key takeaways

  • Yes — you can get a business credit card with no revenue. Issuers approve on your personal credit and income, not business sales.
  • A personal FICO score around 670+ is the practical approval bar; you can enter $0 in the revenue field as a startup.
  • Expect to sign a personal guarantee (you repay if the business can't).
  • Want no personal credit check? Use a secured business card (deposit = limit) or a startup/corporate card that approves on cash-on-hand.
  • First open a business checking account and build business credit with your EIN — it strengthens future approvals.

Best Business Credit Cards for New Companies (No Revenue)

Starting a company with little or no revenue doesn’t have to block your access to business credit. Many entrepreneurs need a card to pay for supplies, marketing, or travel before their first sales. This guide explains realistic card options, practical application strategies, and credit-building steps so you can get a business credit card for a new business with no revenue.

Quick overview: How you can qualify without business income

  • Apply using your personal credit (Social Security number) as a sole proprietor. Issuers often base the decision on personal credit history if the business has no revenue or EIN history.
  • Use secured business cards that accept a cash deposit as the credit line. These are specifically designed for applicants without established business credit or income.
  • Consider corporate cards tailored to startups (like Brex or Ramp) — some accept new companies with no revenue if you have sufficient personal liquidity or funding, though requirements vary.
  • Leverage personal cards for business spending initially, then transition to business cards once your business profile strengthens.

Best card types and specific card options

Below are practical categories and representative card options that are most accessible to startups and sole proprietors with little or no business revenue.

1. Business cards that approve based on personal credit

These are the most common route for new business owners. Cards evaluate your personal credit score, income (personal or business), and credit history.

  • Chase Ink Business Preferred / Ink Business Cash — Good rewards and welcome offers. Chase is strict about recent account openings and requires solid personal credit. Apply as a sole proprietor using your SSN.
  • Capital One Spark Classic for Business — Easier approval if personal credit isn’t perfect (but still expect a fair credit score requirement). Good for basic business needs.
  • American Express Blue Business Cash — Flexible purchasing power and Amex’s small business features. Amex considers personal creditworthiness for new businesses.

Tip: When applying as a sole proprietor, list “sole proprietor” as the business type and put your name as the business owner. Use your SSN when the form asks for tax ID if you don’t have an EIN yet.

2. Secured business credit cards

If you have weak credit or no credit history, secured business cards are reliable. They require a deposit equal to the credit line, minimizing issuer risk.

  • Secured business card options — Fewer mainstream banks offer secured business cards than secured personal cards, but community banks and online issuers occasionally provide them. Check local bank offerings or credit unions if national issuers decline you.
  • Advantages — Easier approval, builds business-specific credit records if the issuer reports to business credit bureaus.

3. Corporate/startup cards that can work with no revenue

New fintech corporate cards may approve startups with little or no revenue depending on other signals like personal credit, company funding, or bank balances.

  • Brex — Known for startup-friendly underwriting. Brex historically approved companies without personal guarantees if founders had sufficient cash in business accounts or venture backing. Policies change, so check current underwriting requirements.
  • Ramp — Offers corporate-style card with built-in expense controls. Ramp typically looks at business banking cash flow and operational metrics rather than traditional revenue figures.

Important: These issuers may require a business bank account, some deposits, or evidence of funding. If you have startup capital (personal savings moved to a business account), that can be sufficient to qualify.

How to apply when your company has no revenue: step-by-step

Follow these steps to maximize approval chances:

  1. Decide the structure and tax ID — If you’re a sole proprietor, you can apply with your SSN. If you have an LLC or corporation, get an EIN (Employer Identification Number) from the IRS. Even without revenue, an EIN and business bank account make you look more legitimate.
  2. Open a business bank account — Move personal startup capital into a business checking account. Issuers like to see funds and transactions, which can substitute for ongoing revenue.
  3. Check your personal credit — Pull your credit report and fix major errors. Most issuers will consider your personal FICO/credit score for a business application when your business has no revenue.
  4. Prepare documentation — Have your EIN (if available), business name and address, personal SSN, and bank statements handy. Some issuers may request projected revenue or expected monthly spend.
  5. Start with more accessible cards — If you have limited credit history, apply for a secured business card or a business card known for easier approvals. Avoid immediately applying to the strictest issuers.
  6. Be honest on the application — Report your actual revenue (even $0 if that’s the case). Misrepresenting income can lead to account closure or fraud flags.
  7. Use the card responsibly — Keep utilization low, pay on time, and gradually increase spending to build a track record. Consider adding yourself as an authorized user on an established business card to build history.

Practical tips and examples

  • Example: Sole proprietor with strong personal credit — If you have a 720+ FICO score but no business revenue, apply for business cards that underwrite on personal credit (Chase Ink, Amex). Use SSN and projected revenue fields to show expected monthly spend.
  • Example: Early-stage founder with savings but no revenue — Move savings to a business checking account, then try fintech corporate cards (Brex, Ramp) that consider bank balances. Alternatively, apply for a business card using personal credit.
  • Example: Founder with poor credit or thin history — Opt for secured business cards or get a co-signer/authorized user on someone else’s account temporarily while building credit.
  • Leverage vendor credit — Start with vendor accounts that extend net-30 terms (e.g., suppliers, trade vendors) to build a credit history and then apply for a card after 3–6 months of payments.

Building business credit when there’s no revenue

Getting a card is only the start. Use these steps to build a trackable business credit profile:

  • Open accounts with vendors that report to business credit bureaus (Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, Equifax Business).
  • Request a DUNS number and make timely vendor payments to establish a PAYDEX score with Dun & Bradstreet.
  • Keep separate business finances—use the business card for business purchases only and pay balances on time.
  • Gradually add authorized users and apply for small increases or new cards as revenue begins.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Misrepresenting income — Listing false revenue can lead to denial or account closure. Use accurate numbers or conservative projections.
  • Assuming revenue is always required — Many issuers underwrite using personal credit or bank balances. If you’re a sole proprietor, your SSN and personal income matter more than business revenue early on.
  • Applying to every card at once — Multiple hard inquiries in a short period can hurt approval odds. Space applications and target ones that match your profile.
  • Mixing personal and business finances — It’s tempting at launch, but mixing accounts makes underwriting murkier and undermines business credit-building.
  • Expecting instant high credit limits — New businesses typically get modest limits at first. Build credit history to qualify for higher lines later.

Checklist before you apply

  • Do you have a personal credit score of ~650+? If not, consider secured options or credit improvement.
  • Do you have an EIN and business bank account? If not, consider applying as a sole proprietor with your SSN or open an EIN quickly.
  • Have you prepared recent personal bank statements or evidence of startup capital?
  • Have you checked which bureaus the issuer uses (personal vs. business) and their typical requirements?
  • Are you ready to keep business spending and payments separate and timely?

When to consider personal credit cards for business use

In many early-stage startups, the fastest path is to use a personal card for business expenses temporarily. Choose a card with robust purchase protections and track expenses carefully for tax and accounting purposes. Plan to transition to a business card within 6–12 months to build distinct business credit.

Final thoughts: realistic expectations and next steps

Getting the best business credit cards for new business with no revenue is very possible if you apply strategically. The most reliable routes are:

  • Applying with your personal credit as a sole proprietor
  • Using secured business cards if you have limited credit
  • Leveraging fintech corporate cards if you have business bank account balances or funding

Start by organizing business paperwork (EIN, bank account), checking your personal credit, and choosing issuers that match your profile. Use small, consistent charges and pay on time to build business credit quickly. Avoid misrepresentation and too many applications at once. With a careful approach, you’ll secure a card that helps your startup grow even before revenue arrives.

Frequently asked questions

Is applying for a business credit card with no revenue hard?

No. Applying for a business credit card with no revenue works like any card application: you enter $0 revenue, the issuer checks your personal credit and income, and you sign a personal guarantee.

Can you get a business credit card with no revenue?

Yes. Most issuers approve based on your personal credit and income, so you can enter $0 business revenue and still qualify by signing a personal guarantee. Major issuers confirm this.

What credit score do you need for a business credit card with no revenue?

A personal FICO score of about 670 or higher is the practical bar for most personal-guarantee business cards. Secured business cards accept lower or limited scores.

Can an LLC with no income get a credit card?

Yes — a brand-new LLC with no income can apply. Approval rests on the owner's personal credit and income, not the LLC's sales, and you'll typically sign a personal guarantee.

Do you have to enter revenue on a business credit card application?

You enter your business revenue, but $0 (or a realistic projection) is acceptable for a startup. Issuers weigh your personal income and credit far more heavily at this stage.

Can you get a business card with no personal guarantee?

Rarely for brand-new companies. No-personal-guarantee cards (startup/corporate cards) usually require meaningful cash in a linked business bank account or investor funding.

title: Best Business Credit Cards for a New LLC (2026)
content:
A new LLC has no business credit history, so card issuers judge the owner, not the company. Most new LLCs are approved on the owner's personal credit and income, with a personal guarantee, even with zero business revenue. This guide explains which card types actually accept a brand-new LLC, what documents to prepare, and how to use the first card to start building business credit.



Key takeaways

  • A new LLC can get a business credit card using the owner's personal credit and a personal guarantee.
  • You don't need business revenue — issuers approve on personal income and credit.
  • A business card separates expenses and helps build business credit when it reports to business bureaus.
  • Start with a no-annual-fee card and pay in full to avoid interest.

Personal-guarantee business cardPersonal credit$0-95Most new LLCs
