Best Business Credit Cards for New LLCs (No Credit?)

Forming an LLC is an important step in separating your personal finances from your business. But if your newly formed LLC has little or no credit history, you may be unsure how to get a business credit card that will help you manage cash flow and build business credit. This guide explains the practical options for the best business credit cards for new LLC with no credit history, how to qualify, and step-by-step strategies to build credit quickly and responsibly.

Why a business card matters for a new LLC

  • Separates personal and business expenses for taxes and bookkeeping.
  • Helps build a credit profile for the business, unlocking better financing later.
  • Provides short-term cash flow and benefits like rewards, purchase protections, and vendor payment terms.
  • Makes spending transparent for partners, investors, and accountants.

But a new LLC without a business credit history faces hurdles. Issuers want to evaluate risk. That means you’ll need to know the realistic card types and the application steps that work for startups with no credit.

Quick overview: Your realistic card choices

If your LLC has limited or no business credit, these are the most common and practical card categories to consider:

  • Secured business credit cards: Require a cash deposit that becomes your credit line. These are the most reliable option for an LLC with no credit history.
  • Small-business starter cards that accept personal guarantees: Many business cards can be approved based on the owner’s personal credit score and income. Good when a founder has fair-to-good personal credit.
  • Business cards from fintech/corporate card providers that underwrite on revenue: Some modern providers approve accounts based on business bank account activity and revenue instead of long credit history — useful for revenue-generating startups.
  • Corporate cards for new businesses with limited credit history: These are sometimes available if the company has a corporate relationship with a bank or an investor backing, but traditional corporate cards usually need established business credit or a guarantee.

How to get a business credit card for a new LLC: step-by-step

1. Decide whether you’ll use a personal guarantee

Most business credit cards require a personal guarantee from an owner, meaning the owner is personally responsible if the business can’t pay. If you’re willing to provide a personal guarantee and you have decent personal credit, you’ll have many more options. If you want to avoid a personal guarantee, you’ll be limited to cards from providers that underwrite to business revenue or secured business cards that accept a deposit.

2. Gather documents and set up basic business infrastructure

  • Employer Identification Number (EIN) — obtain from the IRS.
  • Business bank account opened in the LLC’s name.
  • Articles of Organization/Certificate of Formation and operating agreement.
  • Business phone number, email, and website (even a simple one).

Having these items ready signals legitimacy and helps issuers verify your company quickly.

3. Choose the right card type for your situation

Match the card type to your credit status:

  • If you have little or no personal and business credit: look into secured business credit cards or corporate cards from fintech providers that approve based on bank account history.
  • If you have fair-to-excellent personal credit: many starter business cards accept a personal guarantee; you'll likely qualify for cards with more perks and higher limits.
  • If your business already has some revenue and a stable bank history: consider card products that evaluate cash flow instead of credit history (expense-management cards and some corporate cards).

4. Apply strategically

When applying, be prepared to:

  • Provide EIN, business bank account info, and formation documents.
  • Supply personal information and consent to a personal credit pull if required.
  • Disclose business revenue and time in business — some issuers will approve young businesses with sufficient monthly deposits.

Avoid applying to multiple cards at once — too many hard inquiries can hurt your personal credit and reduce approval odds.

5. Use the card to build business credit

Once you have a card, treat it like a credit-building tool:

  • Keep utilization low (under 30% of the limit).
  • Pay on time or early — payment history is the most important factor.
  • Ask the issuer to report your account to business credit bureaus (Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, Equifax Business). Not all cards report automatically.
  • Establish multiple trade lines over time: vendor accounts, net-30 vendors, and small loans help diversify business credit.

Types of cards explained (pros and cons)

Secured business credit cards for new LLC

How they work: You deposit cash as collateral, and the lender sets your credit limit equal to or slightly higher than that deposit.

  • Pros: Easier approval for businesses with no history; builds credit when issuer reports; predictable limit based on deposit.
  • Cons: Requires upfront cash; may have fewer perks and lower limits; not all secured cards report to business credit bureaus.

Business cards that accept a personal guarantee

How they work: The owner pledges personal responsibility for the account. Issuers use the owner’s personal credit score to qualify.

  • Pros: Access to mainstream business cards with rewards and higher limits; can be obtained by owners with good personal credit even if the LLC is new.
  • Cons: Risks owner’s personal credit; can be harder to separate personal liability.

Corporate/fintech cards that underwrite on revenue

How they work: Some modern card providers look at business bank deposits, recurring revenue, and cash flow instead of just credit history. They may offer cards without a personal guarantee to qualifying companies.

  • Pros: No or limited personal guarantee; approval based on business performance; often include spend controls and integrations for scaling startups.
  • Cons: Usually require consistent deposits and a business bank relationship; may limit options for very early-stage companies with no revenue.

Best starter business cards for small business owners — practical examples

Rather than a one-size-fits-all “best” card, choose based on your situation:

  • If you have low personal credit and little business history: start with a secured business credit card from a reputable bank that reports to business credit agencies.
  • If you have good personal credit: apply for beginner-friendly business cards that accept personal guarantees — these often include simple cash-back or low-fee options.
  • If your startup already has monthly revenue: explore modern corporate/fintech cards that evaluate cash flow and may not require a personal guarantee.

When comparing specific offers, look for annual fees, reporting to business bureaus, introductory APRs, rewards that match your spending, and whether the card requires or avoids a personal guarantee.

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Mistake: Applying for many cards at once. That causes multiple hard inquiries and can lower approval odds.
  • Misconception: “I can’t get a business card until the LLC has years of history.” Not true — secured cards, personal-guarantee cards, and fintech options exist precisely for new businesses.
  • Mistake: Not separating personal and business expenses. Mixing them makes it harder to build clean business credit and complicates taxes.
  • Misconception: “Business cards don't affect personal credit.” Many business cards do require a personal guarantee and can appear on personal credit reports if the company defaults.
  • Mistake: Focusing only on perks. For a new LLC, the priority should be credit reporting, approval odds, and manageable terms rather than high-end rewards.

Checklist: Before you apply

  • Obtain an EIN and open a business bank account.
  • Register your business with state and local authorities.
  • Gather personal ID and business formation documents.
  • Check your personal credit report and fix errors.
  • Decide whether you’ll provide a personal guarantee.
  • Choose the card category that fits your credit and revenue profile.
  • Confirm the issuer reports to business credit bureaus.

How to build business credit quickly after approval

Getting a card is only the start. To create a strong business credit profile:

  • Use the card for regular, planned business expenses — payroll, supplies, subscriptions — and pay the statement in full each month.
  • Keep utilization low and avoid maxing out the card, even if you have a large limit.
  • Request credit limit increases occasionally as revenue grows; higher limits with the same balance lower utilization.
  • Establish vendor credit lines with suppliers who report to business bureaus (trade credit). Net-30 vendors can be a fast way to add tradelines.
  • Monitor business credit scores (Dun & Bradstreet PAYDEX, Experian Business, Equifax Business) and address inaccuracies quickly.

When to transition from starter cards to traditional business financing

As your LLC establishes history and revenue, aim to graduate to cards and loans that don’t require personal guarantees and that offer better terms for established businesses. Milestones to watch for:

  • Consistent revenue and monthly cash flow over 6–12 months.
  • Multiple business tradelines reporting positive payment history.
  • A business credit score that meets lender thresholds (varies by bureau).
  • Strong banking relationships or investor backing.

Summary — Which option is right for your new LLC?

If you’re searching for the best business credit cards for new LLC with no credit history, pick the route that matches your current situation:

  • Very little personal or business credit: start with a secured business credit card that reports to business bureaus.
  • Good personal credit but new LLC: apply for starter business cards that accept personal guarantees to get rewards and higher limits.
  • Revenue-generating startup: explore fintech and corporate card providers that underwrite on cash flow and business banking history.

Whatever path you choose, focus first on building reliable payment history and ensuring that issuers report to the business credit bureaus. Over time, responsible use will open doors to unsecured corporate cards, higher limits, and traditional business financing.

If you’d like, tell me whether you have personal credit history or monthly business revenue, and I’ll suggest specific card features and next steps tailored to your situation.

Frequently asked questions

Can a new LLC get a credit card?

Yes. A new LLC can get a business credit card based on the owner's personal credit and income, typically with a personal guarantee — business revenue isn't required.

Do you need revenue for a business credit card as an LLC?

No. You can enter $0 or projected revenue; issuers weigh your personal income and credit far more heavily for a new LLC.

Does an LLC need an EIN for a business credit card?

A single-member LLC can sometimes apply with an SSN, but an EIN is free, common for business cards, and required if you have employees.

Do you have to sign a personal guarantee?

For most new LLCs, yes. A personal guarantee makes you personally responsible if the business can't pay, which is how issuers manage the risk.

Does a business credit card build business credit?

It can, if the card reports to business credit bureaus. Pay on time and keep utilization low to build a strong business credit file.

title: How to Open a Business Bank Account Without an EIN
content:
Reviewed by the Learner's Link editorial team · Last updated: September 2026
Researched from official sources including IRS: apply for an EIN (free) and SBA: open a business bank account. We accept no payment to feature specific providers.

Key takeaways

  • Sole proprietors can open a business bank account using their SSN instead of an EIN at many banks.
  • Typically you need: a government photo ID, your SSN, and a business name (or you trade under your own name).
  • An EIN is free from the IRS and takes minutes online — getting one is optional for sole proprietors but recommended for privacy.
  • LLCs, partnerships, and any business with employees do need an EIN to open an account.
  • Related: see our guides on build business credit with your EIN and no-fee business checking for freelancers.

Do you need an EIN to open a business account?

Business typeEIN required?Can use SSN?
Sole proprietor (no employees)NoYes
Single-member LLCUsually yesSometimes
Partnership / multi-member LLCYesNo
Any business with employeesYesNo

Open a Business Bank Account Without an EIN

Starting a small business as a sole proprietor often raises the question: can you open a business bank account without an EIN? The short answer is yes. Many banks let sole proprietors open a business bank account using their Social Security Number (SSN) instead of an Employer Identification Number (EIN). This guide walks you through why you might choose to do this, step-by-step instructions, which banks commonly allow it, documents needed, options while your EIN is pending, and common mistakes to avoid.

Why open a separate business bank account as a sole proprietor?

  • Keep personal and business finances separate: Separating accounts simplifies bookkeeping and tax preparation, and makes it easier to track business income and expenses.
  • Build credibility with customers and vendors: Accepting checks or payments in a business account looks more professional.
  • Protect personal liability and financial organization: While a sole proprietor doesn’t have the liability protection of an LLC, separation reduces the risk of commingling funds and clarifies business performance.
  • Access to business tools: Business accounts often include merchant services, payroll options, and business debit/credit cards.

Can you open a business bank account without an EIN?

Yes. Most banks will allow a sole proprietor to open a business checking or savings account using an SSN in place of an EIN. The bank typically treats the account as a “sole proprietorship” account and uses your name and SSN for tax reporting (1099s, interest statements, etc.).

However, policies vary by bank and sometimes by branch or account type. Larger national banks commonly accept SSNs for sole proprietors, while some business-only accounts or accounts with specific features may require an EIN.

Step-by-step: How to open a business bank account without an EIN

1. Decide what type of account you need

Choose between a basic business checking account, a business savings account, or a combined package. Think about monthly transaction limits, fees, minimum balances, online banking, and merchant services.

2. Gather required documents

Most banks will require a combination of the following when you open a sole proprietor business bank account with an SSN:

  • Valid government-issued photo ID (driver’s license, passport, state ID)
  • Social Security Number (SSN) or Social Security card — many banks accept the SSN printed on your ID, but some may ask to see the Social Security card
  • Proof of business name
    • If you operate under your legal name (e.g., Jane Doe doing business as Jane Doe), a separate DBA may not be required.
    • If you use a trade name, bring a "Doing Business As" (DBA) or fictitious name filing from your county or state.
  • Business license or permit, if your city or state requires one for your type of business
  • Business address (a home address is acceptable for sole proprietors)
  • Estimated annual revenue and anticipated monthly transactions (banks often ask these for account setup)

3. Compare banks and account terms

Shop for features that matter to you: monthly fees, fee waivers, free transactions, ATM access, mobile deposit, integrations with accounting software, and customer service. If you plan to accept card payments, check merchant service options and fees.

4. Apply in person or online

Many banks allow online account opening, but for sole proprietors using an SSN and a DBA you may prefer visiting a branch. In-person visits can be smoother if the bank requests any local filings or if staff need to verify DBA paperwork.

5. Fund the account and set up services

Bring enough to meet the minimum opening deposit. Once open, order checks, request a business debit card, enroll in online banking, and set up any merchant services or bill pay needed.

Banks that commonly allow business accounts without an EIN

Policies change, but the following bank types and specific banks often allow sole proprietors to open business accounts using an SSN instead of an EIN:

  • Large national banks: Bank of America, Chase, Wells Fargo, and Citibank typically permit sole proprietors to open business checking with SSN. Requirements vary by account tier and branch.
  • Regional banks and credit unions: Many regional banks and credit unions accept SSNs for sole proprietors and can be a good option for more personalized service.
  • Online banks and fintechs: Online business banks and fintech platforms (such as BlueVine, Novo, Mercury for certain solo founders) often allow account opening with SSN, though some fintechs require an EIN for certain business entity types.

Tip: Check each bank’s account disclosures or call customer service to confirm policy changes and documentation requirements before visiting or applying.

Open a business account with SSN instead of EIN: what to expect

  • Tax reporting: Banks will report interest and other taxable items to the IRS using your SSN.
  • Privacy considerations: Using an SSN ties the account directly to your personal taxpayer identity. If you later form an LLC or obtain an EIN, you can request to update the account to the new business EIN.
  • Credit and lending: Business credit history may be limited initially. Some lenders consider personal credit history for sole proprietors who use SSNs.

EIN pending? Options for opening an account

If you applied for an EIN but haven’t received it yet, some banks will allow you to open the account and update the EIN later. Options include:

  • Open with SSN, update later: Start the account with your SSN and bring the EIN paperwork when it’s issued to update the account records.
  • Bring IRS application receipt: If you applied online or by fax, bring documentation or an EIN application confirmation; some banks will accept proof that your EIN is pending.
  • Wait for EIN issuance: If you prefer, you can wait; obtaining an EIN online from the IRS is typically immediate if you apply on the IRS website.

Note: If banks require an EIN for certain services (like payroll accounts or multiple-signature accounts), ask if you can open a basic account first and upgrade once the EIN is issued.

Documents needed to open a business bank account as a sole proprietor (quick checklist)

  • Primary photo ID (driver’s license, passport)
  • Social Security Number (SSN) or card
  • DBA/Fictitious name filing (if using a trade name)
  • Business license or permit (if applicable)
  • Business address and contact details
  • Initial deposit (check or cash)

Common mistakes and misconceptions to avoid

  • Assuming all banks treat sole proprietors the same: Policies vary—call ahead or read disclosures to confirm SSN acceptance and documents required.
  • Using personal accounts for business: Mixing finances complicates taxes and can hurt professional image. Open a separate business account even as a sole proprietor.
  • Not getting a DBA when needed: If you operate under a trade name different from your legal name, failing to register a DBA can lead to compliance or acceptance issues at the bank.
  • Delaying EIN if you plan to hire or add employees: You’ll need an EIN to hire employees and for certain tax filings—get one before you recruit staff.
  • Missing account fees and limits: Carefully check monthly fees, transaction limits, and fee waivers to avoid unexpected charges.

Practical tips and examples

  • Example workflow: Sarah runs a freelance graphic design business as a sole proprietor. She registers a DBA with her county, compares two local banks, visits a branch with her ID, SSN, DBA certificate, and $100 opening deposit, and opens a business checking account that integrates with her invoicing software.
  • Consider a business debit card: Use a business debit card for business purchases to keep records tidy. Request a card when opening the account.
  • Ask about online accounting integrations: Choose a bank that integrates with QuickBooks, Xero, or your invoicing app to save bookkeeping time.
  • If you run a home-based business: Your home address is typically acceptable; if you worry about privacy, consider a registered agent service for an LLC later or a P.O. Box in addition to the physical address requirement (banks often need a physical address for identity verification).

When to get an EIN anyway

Even though you can open a sole proprietor business bank account without an EIN, applying for one is often free and simple via the IRS website. Consider getting an EIN if you:

  • Plan to hire employees
  • Want to separate your SSN from business transactions for privacy
  • Are forming an LLC, partnership, or corporation
  • Need account features that some banks restrict to entities with EINs

Conclusion

Opening a sole proprietor business bank account without an EIN is a common and achievable step for new business owners. Most banks accept an SSN in place of an EIN for sole proprietorships, provided you bring primary ID, proof of your business name (DBA if applicable), and any local licenses. Compare banks for fee structure, features, and integrations. If you anticipate hiring or want further separation between your personal and business tax identity, obtain an EIN—either before or shortly after opening your account. Separating your finances early makes taxes, bookkeeping, and growth easier, so take the step now even if you don’t yet have an EIN.

Frequently asked questions

Can I open a business bank account without an EIN?

Yes, if you're a sole proprietor. Many banks let you open a business account with your SSN, a photo ID, and your business name. LLCs and employers need an EIN.

Do I need an EIN as a sole proprietor?

Not to open an account, but an EIN is free from the IRS, protects your SSN privacy, and is required if you hire employees or form an LLC.

What documents do I need to open a business bank account?

Generally a government photo ID, your SSN or EIN, and your business name or registration. Requirements vary by bank and business structure.

How long does it take to get an EIN?

Applying online through the IRS takes only a few minutes, and you receive the EIN immediately at the end of the session — at no cost.

Is it worth separating business and personal banking?

Yes. It simplifies taxes, makes bookkeeping cleaner, and supports the liability protection of an LLC if you form one later.
